locator: I q.13 a.5 co.: quidquid dicitur de Deo et creaturis, dicitur secundum quod est aliquis ordo creaturae ad Deum, ut ad principium et causam, in qua praeexistunt excellenter omnes rerum perfectiones
interpretation: Read for one perfection said of God and of creatures: every other thing that has it has it by its order to the primary as to its principle and cause, that is, the primary is a cause of that perfection in it (CausesIn p x r). The sentence grounds the community of the name in that order; the reading takes the order 'ut ad causam' to presuppose that the causal relation obtains, which is the reading choice (DISAMB-CAUSE: cause of a perfection, not mover). It is the second of the two modes of analogy the article distinguishes (one to another, as medicine to the animal's health), not the first (many to one). Only the instance r = esse is used by the results. Aristotle's pros hen (ARIST-MET-1003A-BEING-SAID-PROS-HEN-A) does not give it: there the relation to the primary may be being an affection, a way, a privation of substance, not only being caused by it.
